ctx.en: Until the business got going, I worked without a day off.

ctx.s: 「新事業[しんじぎょう]はいかがですか」「おかげさまで、ようやく{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]りました}」
ctx.en: "How is the new venture?" "Thank you, it's finally up and running."

ctx.s: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]して半年[はんとし]、新[あたら]しい生活[せいかつ]がようやく{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]った}。
ctx.en: Six months after the move, my new life has finally settled into a routine.

ctx.s: まずはこのプロジェクトを{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]せる}ことが先決[せんけつ]だ。
ctx.en: The first priority is to get this project on track.

ctx.s: 復興計画[ふっこうけいかく]が{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]る}には、なお数年[すうねん]かかる見通[みとお]しだ。
ctx.en: It is expected to take several more years for the reconstruction plan to get properly under way.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は褒[ほ]められて{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]り}、自慢[じまん]ばかりしている。
bad.en: (meant: he got carried away after being praised and keeps boasting)
bad.why: Getting cocky is choshi ni noru; this idiom is about a project running smoothly, not a person's mood.

bad.s: 電車[でんしゃ]に遅[おく]れそうだったので、急[いそ]いで{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I was about to miss the train, so I hurried and got on)
bad.why: It is figurative, about undertakings settling down; boarding a train is simply densha ni noru.

cards.mean: to warn someone in advance
cards.lit: to drive in a nail: fixing something firmly so that it cannot shift later

use.how: The person warned takes に: 〜に〜ないように釘を刺す. A firm warning beforehand so that they will not do something one fears they might.

near.diff: 念を押す just confirms a point to avoid a mix-up; 釘を刺す warns someone off something one suspects they will do.

cards.cue: Your brother always spreads your secrets. Before telling him your news, you warn him sharply not to breathe a word of it. What did you do?

ctx.s: 母[はは]に「今度[こんど]は無駄遣[むだづか]いしないでね」と{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]された}。
ctx.en: My mother warned me: "Don't waste your money this time."

ctx.s: 「このことは誰[だれ]にも言[い]わないでよ」と、口[くち]の軽[かる]い友達[ともだち]に{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]して}おいた。
ctx.en: I warned my loose-lipped friend beforehand: "Don't tell anyone about this."

ctx.s: 「また飲[の]みすぎないでよ」「わかってるって。そんなに{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]さなくても}いいよ」
ctx.en: "Don't drink too much again." "I know. You don't have to warn me like that."

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は遅刻[ちこく]の多[おお]い彼[かれ]に、明日[あした]は遅[おく]れるなと{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]した}。
ctx.en: The manager warned him, since he is often late, not to be late tomorrow.

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]は試合前[しあいまえ]、選手[せんしゅ]たちに油断[ゆだん]するなと{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]した}。
ctx.en: Before the match, the coach warned the players not to get complacent.

ctx.s: 大家[おおや]さんは入居者[にゅうきょしゃ]に、夜中[よなか]に騒[さわ]がないようにと{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]した}。
ctx.en: The landlord warned the tenants not to make noise late at night.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]は合格[ごうかく]した生徒[せいと]に「おめでとう」と{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]した}。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher told the student who passed "congratulations")
bad.why: It is a warning against doing something; congratulations or praise is never a warning.

bad.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は部下[ぶか]を{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]した}。
bad.en: (meant: the manager warned his subordinate)
bad.why: The person warned takes ni, not o: buka ni kugi o sasu. Two o-objects in a row is ungrammatical.

cards.mean: to stress a point again to make sure it is understood
cards.lit: to press one's thought home: nen is a concern held in mind, pressed firmly onto the listener

use.how: With a quotation or clause: 「〜ね」と念を押す, 〜に念を押す. Repeating or confirming a point, such as a time or a promise, so that there is no mistake.

near.diff: 釘を刺す is a pre-emptive warning against bad behaviour; 念を押す is neutral checking that something is understood or agreed.

cards.cue: Before hanging up, you repeat to the courier once more that the parcel must arrive by ten tomorrow, just to be sure. What did you do?

ctx.s: 「明日[あした]は八時[はちじ]集合[しゅうごう]だよ」と{念[ねん]を押[お]した}。
ctx.en: "We meet at eight tomorrow, remember," I reminded them.

ctx.s: 出[で]かける前[まえ]に、妻[つま]に「鍵[かぎ]、閉[し]めたよね？」と{念[ねん]を押[お]された}。
ctx.en: Before we went out, my wife made sure: "You locked the door, right?"

ctx.s: 「本当[ほんとう]に大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]？」と、彼[かれ]は何度[なんど]も{念[ねん]を押[お]した}。
ctx.en: "Are you really sure it's all right?" he asked again and again.

ctx.s: 店員[てんいん]は「返品[へんぴん]はできませんが、よろしいですか」と{念[ねん]を押[お]した}。
ctx.en: The clerk checked once more: "Returns aren't possible. Is that all right?"

ctx.s: 「締[し]め切[き]りは金曜日[きんようび]で間違[まちが]いないですね」と{念[ねん]を押[お]す}と、担当者[たんとうしゃ]はうなずいた。
ctx.en: When I double-checked, "The deadline is definitely Friday, isn't it?", the person in charge nodded.

ctx.s: 契約[けいやく]の前[まえ]に、条件[じょうけん]に変更[へんこう]がないか{念[ねん]を押[お]して}おいた。
ctx.en: Before signing, I made sure once more that the terms had not changed.

bad.s: エレベーターのボタンを{念[ねん]を押[お]した}。
bad.en: (meant: I pressed the lift button)
bad.why: Pressing a button is botan o osu; this idiom is only about confirming a point with someone.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]の結果[けっか]が心配[しんぱい]で、一晩中[ひとばんじゅう]{念[ねん]を押[お]した}。
bad.en: (meant: I was so anxious about my results that I worried all night)
bad.why: It is said to someone to confirm a point; it does not mean to fret or worry alone.

cards.mean: not worth the trouble or cost
cards.lit: does not square with its share: what comes back does not match what is put in

use.how: Predicate about a job, deal or effort: この仕事は割に合わない. Says the reward is too small for the effort, risk or cost involved.

cards.cue: A part-time job means long night shifts and heavy lifting, yet pays barely above the minimum. How do you sum it up?

ctx.s: こんなに大変[たいへん]なのに時給[じきゅう]がこれでは、{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}。
ctx.en: It's this hard and pays only this much an hour? It isn't worth it.

ctx.s: 往復[おうふく]三時間[さんじかん]かけて安[やす]いスーパーに行[い]くのは、{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}よ。
ctx.en: Spending three hours there and back to go to a cheap supermarket isn't worth it.

ctx.s: 「その依頼[いらい]、受[う]けるの？」「手間[てま]ばかりかかって{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}から、断[ことわ]るよ」
ctx.en: "Are you taking that job?" "It's all hassle and doesn't pay, so I'm turning it down."

ctx.s: 危険[きけん]な仕事[しごと]なのに給料[きゅうりょう]が安[やす]く、{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}と辞[や]める人[ひと]が多[おお]い。
ctx.en: The work is dangerous but the pay is low, so many people quit, saying it isn't worth it.

ctx.s: 罰金[ばっきん]の額[がく]を考[かんが]えれば、駐車違反[ちゅうしゃいはん]は{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}。
ctx.en: Given the size of the fine, parking illegally just doesn't pay.

ctx.s: 小[ちい]さな農家[のうか]にとって、この作物[さくもつ]を育[そだ]てるのは{割[わり]に合[あ]わなく}なっている。
ctx.en: For small farmers, growing this crop is no longer worth the cost.

bad.s: この服[ふく]は、サイズが{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}。
bad.en: (meant: these clothes don't fit me)
bad.why: It weighs reward against effort or cost; clothes that do not fit are simply saizu ga awanai.

bad.s: 思[おも]ったより{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}点数[てんすう]が取[と]れて、とても嬉[うれ]しかった。
bad.en: (meant: I got a better score than I deserved and was delighted)
bad.why: It only says the return falls short of the effort; it never describes a pleasing surprise.

cards.mean: to pay out of one's own pocket
cards.lit: to cut one's own belly: the cost comes out of oneself, not out of someone else's purse

use.how: Said when one pays a cost that a company, school or someone else might have been expected to cover: 自腹を切って買う. Also 自腹で払う.

cards.cue: The company refuses to buy the software the team needs, so the team leader pays for it personally. What did the leader do?

ctx.s: 会社[かいしゃ]の飲[の]み会[かい]なのに、{自腹[じばら]を切[き]る}ことになった。
ctx.en: It was a company party, yet I ended up paying my own way.

ctx.s: 経費[けいひ]で落[お]ちないので、{自腹[じばら]を切[き]って}本[ほん]を買[か]った。
ctx.en: It couldn't go on expenses, so I bought the books with my own money.

ctx.s: 「その参考書[さんこうしょ]、学校[がっこう]が買[か]ってくれたの？」「ううん、{自腹[じばら]を切[き]った}よ」
ctx.en: "Did the school buy you that study guide?" "No, I paid for it myself."

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]は{自腹[じばら]を切[き]って}、生徒[せいと]たちにお菓子[かし]を配[くば]った。
ctx.en: The teacher bought sweets for the pupils out of their own pocket.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]が{自腹[じばら]を切[き]って}、チーム全員[ぜんいん]に夕食[ゆうしょく]をごちそうしてくれた。
ctx.en: The department head treated the whole team to dinner out of their own pocket.

ctx.s: 授業[じゅぎょう]で使[つか]う教材[きょうざい]を、{自腹[じばら]を切[き]って}用意[ようい]する教員[きょういん]も少[すく]なくない。
ctx.en: Quite a few teachers pay out of their own pockets for the materials they use in class.

bad.s: 友達[ともだち]におごってもらって、{自腹[じばら]を切[き]った}。
bad.en: (meant: my friend treated me, so I didn't pay)
bad.why: It means paying with your own money; when someone else pays for you, you have not paid out of your own pocket.

bad.s: ミスの責任[せきにん]を取[と]って、彼[かれ]は{自腹[じばら]を切[き]って}会社[かいしゃ]を辞[や]めた。
bad.en: (meant: he took responsibility for the mistake and resigned)
bad.why: It is only about paying with one's own money; taking the blame and resigning is sekinin o toru, not this phrase.

cards.mean: ominous, an unlucky thing to say
cards.lit: not even a matter of omens: so ill-starred it should not be said at all

story.text: Engi began as a Buddhist term, the rendering of the Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda: the teaching that all things arise in dependence on causes and conditions. In Japan the word came to mean the founding story of a temple or shrine, and later a sign of what is to come. Engi ga ii is a good omen; engi de mo nai rejects a remark as so ill-omened it should not be spoken.
story.source: Buddhist term 縁起 (Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda, dependent origination)

use.how: A retort to talk of death, failure or disaster, as if saying it could make it happen: 縁起でもないこと言わないで. Also as a predicate: 〜なんて縁起でもない.

cards.cue: On the morning of a long road trip, a friend starts joking about what would happen if you crashed. You tell them to stop tempting fate.

ctx.s: {縁起[えんぎ]でもない}ことを言[い]わないで。
ctx.en: Don't say such ominous things.

ctx.s: 「試験[しけん]に落[お]ちたらどうしよう」「{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}。大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]だよ」
ctx.en: "What if I fail the exam?" "Don't tempt fate. You'll be fine."

ctx.s: 出発[しゅっぱつ]の朝[あさ]に事故[じこ]の話[はなし]なんて、{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}。
ctx.en: Talking about accidents on the morning we set off? That's asking for bad luck.

ctx.s: 「もしものときのために遺言[ゆいごん]を書[か]いておこうかな」「やめてよ、{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}」
ctx.en: "Maybe I should write a will, just in case." "Stop it, don't even say that."

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]は、お見舞[みま]いに鉢植[はちう]えを持[も]っていくのは{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}と言[い]った。
ctx.en: My grandmother said taking a potted plant to someone in hospital is bad luck.

ctx.s: 受験生[じゅけんせい]の前[まえ]では、「落[お]ちる」のような{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}言葉[ことば]は使[つか]わないようにしている。
ctx.en: In front of students facing entrance exams, I avoid ill-omened words like "fall".

bad.s: 宝[たから]くじが当[あ]たるなんて、{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}！
bad.en: (meant: winning the lottery, what luck!)
bad.why: It rebukes ill-omened talk; good fortune is engi ga ii, never this phrase.

bad.s: 部長[ぶちょう]、その企画[きかく]は{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}と思[おも]います。
bad.en: (meant: sir, I think that plan is a bad idea)
bad.why: It is about words that seem to invite bad luck, not a judgement that a plan is unwise, and it is too blunt for a superior.

cards.r: きゅうしにいっしょうをえる
cards.mean: to have a narrow escape from death
cards.lit: out of nine chances of death, to get the one chance of life

use.how: Predicate, usually past, about a person who survived an accident, disaster or illness that should have killed them: 事故で九死に一生を得た.

near.diff: 危機一髪 names the hair's-breadth moment of danger itself; 九死に一生を得る says someone came through a deadly situation alive.

cards.cue: A climber was buried by an avalanche and dug out alive after a full day under the snow. How do the news reports describe the survival?

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は若[わか]いころ、交通事故[こうつうじこ]で{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}。
ctx.en: When he was young, my father barely survived a car accident.

ctx.s: 雪崩[なだれ]に巻[ま]き込[こ]まれた登山者[とざんしゃ]が、{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}。
ctx.en: A climber caught in an avalanche narrowly escaped death.

ctx.s: 「あの船[ふね]の事故[じこ]で助[たす]かったの？」「うん、まさに{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}よ」
ctx.en: "You survived that boat accident?" "Yes, I really did cheat death."

ctx.s: 心臓[しんぞう]が止[と]まったが、居合[いあ]わせた医師[いし]のおかげで{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}。
ctx.en: His heart stopped, but thanks to a doctor who happened to be there, he survived against the odds.

ctx.s: {九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}経験[けいけん]から、彼[かれ]は命[いのち]の大切[たいせつ]さを語[かた]り続[つづ]けている。
ctx.en: Having escaped death by a whisker, he keeps speaking about how precious life is.

ctx.s: 漁船[ぎょせん]は嵐[あらし]で転覆[てんぷく]したが、乗組員[のりくみいん]は全員[ぜんいん]{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}。
ctx.en: The fishing boat capsized in the storm, but the whole crew narrowly escaped with their lives.

bad.s: 消防士[しょうぼうし]が子[こ]どもを{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}。
bad.en: (meant: the firefighter saved the child)
bad.why: The subject is the person who survived, and the phrase takes no other object; a rescuer saving someone is tasukeru.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]て}、そのまま亡[な]くなった。
bad.en: (meant: he very nearly survived but died)
bad.why: It means one did survive; it cannot be followed by the person's death.

cards.mean: every moment counts
cards.lit: to fight over a single moment: ikkoku, literally one koku of time, here means an instant

use.how: Predicate or modifier about an emergency: 事態は一刻を争う, 一刻を争う状況. Says delay would cause real harm, so there is no time to lose.

cards.cue: A man has collapsed on the station platform and is not breathing. You tell the staff the ambulance cannot wait a single minute.

ctx.s: 患者[かんじゃ]の容体[ようだい]は{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}。
ctx.en: The patient's condition is critical; there's no time to lose.

ctx.s: {一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}状況[じょうきょう]なので、すぐに救急車[きゅうきゅうしゃ]を呼[よ]んでください。
ctx.en: Every second counts, so please call an ambulance right away.

ctx.s: 「明日[あした]まで待[ま]てない？」「だめだ、これは{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}問題[もんだい]なんだ」
ctx.en: "Can't it wait until tomorrow?" "No, this is a matter where every moment counts."

ctx.s: 地震[じしん]の後[あと]、がれきの下[した]の人[ひと]を助[たす]け出[だ]すのは{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}作業[さぎょう]だった。
ctx.en: After the earthquake, getting people out from under the rubble was a race against time.

ctx.s: システムの不具合[ふぐあい]で顧客[こきゃく]データが消[き]えかけており、対応[たいおう]は{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}。
ctx.en: A system fault is about to wipe customer data, so the response cannot wait a moment.

ctx.s: 被災地[ひさいち]への支援[しえん]は{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}と、専門家[せんもんか]は訴[うった]えた。
ctx.en: Experts urged that aid to the disaster area is needed without a moment's delay.

bad.s: 二人[ふたり]は優勝[ゆうしょう]をかけて{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: the two fought it out for the title)
bad.why: Here arasou does not mean competing with a rival; the phrase says a matter is so urgent no time can be lost.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]って}考[かんが]えてから、ゆっくり答[こた]えた。
bad.en: (meant: he thought for a moment and then answered slowly)
bad.why: It does not mean "for a moment"; it describes an emergency where any delay does harm.

cards.mean: to be caught between two sides
cards.lit: to end up pinched between two boards

use.how: Usually AとBの板挟みになる or 二人の間で板挟みになる: said of someone squeezed between two people or groups whose demands clash.

near.diff: 進退きわまる is being stuck with no way forward or back; 板挟みになる is being pulled by two parties whose wishes conflict.

cards.cue: Your boss wants the project done a month early; your team says that is impossible and wants you to tell the boss. You are stuck in the middle.

ctx.en: I'm caught between my mother and my wife, and I really don't know what to do.

ctx.s: 中間[ちゅうかん]管理職[かんりしょく]は、上司[じょうし]と部下[ぶか]の{板挟[いたばさ]みになり}やすい。
ctx.en: Middle managers easily get caught between their bosses and their staff.

ctx.s: 「どっちの味方[みかた]なの？」と聞[き]かれて、二人[ふたり]の友達[ともだち]の間[あいだ]で{板挟[いたばさ]みになった}。
ctx.en: Asked "Whose side are you on?", I found myself caught between my two friends.

ctx.s: 「店長[てんちょう]、大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]ですか」「本社[ほんしゃ]とお客[きゃく]さんの{板挟[いたばさ]みになって}、もう限界[げんかい]だよ」
ctx.en: "Are you all right, manager?" "I'm stuck between head office and the customers, and I've had about all I can take."

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は会社[かいしゃ]と労働[ろうどう]組合[くみあい]の{板挟[いたばさ]みになり}、眠[ねむ]れない日[ひ]が続[つづ]いた。
ctx.en: Caught between the company and the union, he went through night after sleepless night.

ctx.s: 親[おや]の希望[きぼう]と自分[じぶん]の夢[ゆめ]の{板挟[いたばさ]みになった}とき、あなたならどうしますか。
ctx.en: If you were caught between your parents' wishes and your own dream, what would you do?

bad.s: ケーキとアイスのどちらにしようか、{板挟[いたばさ]みになって}迷[まよ]った。
bad.en: (meant: I couldn't decide between cake and ice cream)

bad.en: (meant: I'm under pressure from deadlines)
bad.why: There must be two opposing sides pulling at you; pressure from one source such as a deadline is owareru.

cards.mean: to cause friction
cards.lit: corners stick up: something sharp-edged juts out and grates on the people around it

use.how: Subject is a way of speaking or acting: そう言うと角が立つ. Often in 角が立たないように, about avoiding needless offence to people one deals with.

near.diff: 波風が立つ is trouble stirring in a group or family; 角が立つ is the harsh edge of a particular remark or way of doing something.

cards.cue: You want to decline a neighbour's invitation, but just saying 'I don't want to' would sour things. How would that blunt refusal come across?

ctx.s: そんな言[い]い方[かた]をしたら{角[かど]が立[た]つ}よ。
ctx.en: If you put it like that, you'll rub people the wrong way.

ctx.s: {角[かど]が立[た]たない}ように、やんわりと断[ことわ]った。
ctx.en: I turned it down gently so as not to cause any bad feeling.

ctx.s: 「はっきり言[い]ったほうがいいかな」「でも、それだと{角[かど]が立[た]つ}んじゃない？」
ctx.en: "Should I just say it straight?" "But wouldn't that cause friction?"

ctx.s: 会議[かいぎ]で上司[じょうし]の間違[まちが]いを指摘[してき]すると{角[かど]が立[た]つ}ので、後[あと]で個別[こべつ]に伝[つた]えた。
ctx.en: Pointing out my boss's mistake in the meeting would have caused friction, so I mentioned it privately afterwards.

ctx.s: メールだと冷[つめ]たく読[よ]めて{角[かど]が立[た]つ}こともあるから、電話[でんわ]で話[はな]そう。
ctx.en: In an email it can read as cold and come across badly, so let's talk on the phone.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{角[かど]が立[た]たない}言葉[ことば]を選[えら]ぶのが本当[ほんとう]にうまい。
ctx.en: She's really good at choosing words that don't ruffle anyone.

bad.s: 父[ちち]は朝[あさ]から{角[かど]が立[た]って}いて、誰[だれ]とも話[はな]さない。
bad.en: (meant: my father has been in a bad mood since morning)
bad.why: It describes a remark or action that grates on others, not a person's mood; for a bad mood say kigen ga warui.

bad.en: (meant: the minister's remark caused a nationwide controversy)
bad.why: It is about friction between people who deal with each other; a public uproar over a statement is butsugi o kamosu.

cards.mean: to underestimate, to take lightly
cards.lit: to tie up the total: to settle in advance on how much something will amount to

use.how: Usually 〜と高をくくる or 高をくくっていたら…: assuming something will be easy or harmless, and usually being proved wrong.

near.diff: 甘く見る takes a direct object (相手を甘く見る); 高をくくる is usually a と-clause assumption that something will turn out to be no big deal.

ctx.en: I assumed it would be easy, and then I couldn't do it at all.

ctx.en: Thinking it was just a cold, I didn't bother going to the doctor.

ctx.en: Taking it for granted that it wouldn't rain was my mistake.

ctx.s: 「締[し]め切[き]りまでまだ一週間[いっしゅうかん]あるし」「そうやって{高[たか]をくくって}ると、また徹夜[てつや]になるよ」
ctx.en: "There's still a week until the deadline." "If you take it that lightly, you'll be up all night again."

ctx.s: 相手[あいて]は格下[かくした]だと{高[たか]をくくった}チームは、前半[ぜんはん]だけで三点[さんてん]を奪[うば]われた。
ctx.en: Sure its opponents were weaker, the team gave up three goals in the first half alone.

ctx.s: どうせ誰[だれ]も気[き]づかないと{高[たか]をくくる}のは危険[きけん]だ。
ctx.en: It's dangerous to assume that nobody will notice anyway.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]を{高[たか]をくくって}、宿題[しゅくだい]を出[だ]さなかった。
bad.en: (meant: I underestimated the teacher and didn't hand in my homework)
bad.why: It does not take a person as its object; say sensei o amaku mite, or put the assumption in a to-clause.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は謙虚[けんきょ]で、いつも自分[じぶん]の成果[せいか]を{高[たか]をくくって}話[はな]す。
bad.en: (meant: he's modest and always plays down his achievements)
bad.why: It is a careless assumption that something will be easy, not modestly downplaying oneself.

cards.r: みぎにでるものはいない
cards.mean: no one is better at it
cards.lit: there is no one who comes out on his right

story.text: In Han-dynasty China the right was ranked above the left, so a place on someone's right was a higher place. To say that no one 'comes out on his right' meant that no one ranks above him. The same custom gave the word sasen, 'moving to the left', for a demotion, a word Japanese still uses.
story.source: Classical Chinese 無出其右 and the Han-dynasty custom of ranking right above left

use.how: Usually 〜にかけては Xの右に出る者はいない: high praise that no one surpasses a person in one particular skill or field.

near.diff: 一目置く is the respectful attitude others take toward someone abler; 右に出る者はいない flatly states that no one is better.

cards.cue: Whenever a computer breaks in your office, everyone goes to the same colleague, who always fixes it faster than anyone else could.

ctx.s: 料理[りょうり]にかけては、母[はは]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいない}。
ctx.en: When it comes to cooking, nobody beats my mother.

ctx.s: この町[まち]で寿司[すし]を握[にぎ]らせたら、あの職人[しょくにん]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいない}。
ctx.en: Nobody in this town makes sushi better than that chef.

ctx.s: 「パソコンのことは誰[だれ]に聞[き]けばいい？」「田中[たなか]さんだね。社内[しゃない]で彼[かれ]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいない}よ」
ctx.en: "Who should I ask about computers?" "Tanaka. Nobody in the company knows more than him."

ctx.s: 交渉[こうしょう]のうまさでは、彼女[かのじょ]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいなかった}。
ctx.en: No one could match her skill at negotiating.

ctx.s: 短距離走[たんきょりそう]では、今[いま]のところ彼[かれ]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいない}と言[い]われている。
ctx.en: In sprinting, he is said to have no equal at the moment.

ctx.s: 書道[しょどう]の世界[せかい]において、氏[し]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいない}。
ctx.en: In the world of calligraphy, no one surpasses him.

cards.mean: to give a vague answer to dodge the issue
cards.lit: to make the tea cloudy

near.diff: 言葉を濁す is simply not saying something clearly; お茶を濁す is getting through the moment with a vague or makeshift stand-in.

ctx.s: 政府[せいふ]の答弁[とうべん]は、具体的[ぐたいてき]な数字[すうじ]を示[しめ]さずに{お茶[ちゃ]を濁[にご]す}ものだった。
ctx.en: The government's answer gave no concrete figures and simply skirted the issue.

bad.en: (meant: I said clearly 'I'm not going' and turned it down)

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の冗談[じょうだん]が会議[かいぎ]の雰囲気[ふんいき]を{お茶[ちゃ]を濁[にご]した}。
bad.en: (meant: his joke spoiled the mood of the meeting)
bad.why: It is about dodging a question or task yourself, and it takes no second object; spoiling a mood is mizu o sasu.

cards.mean: to see one's way to finishing
cards.lit: the mark one is aiming at stands up: the goal comes into view

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい部品[ぶひん]が届[とど]いたので、修理[しゅうり]の{めどが立[た]った}と連絡[れんらく]があった。

bad.en: (meant: I've written and handed in the report, so it's finished)

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の顔[かお]を見[み]て、怒[おこ]っている{めどが立[た]った}。
bad.en: (meant: from his face I could tell he was angry)
bad.why: It is about seeing a path to getting something done, not reading someone's feelings; that is sasshi ga tsuku.

cards.mean: to cause controversy
cards.lit: to brew public argument, the way sake is slowly brewed

near.diff: 波紋を呼ぶ is a statement or event sending out ripples of reaction; 物議を醸す stresses that it sets off argument and criticism.

cards.cue: A minister makes an offhand remark about pensioners, and for a week the papers, TV and social media argue over whether it was acceptable.

ctx.s: 大臣[だいじん]の発言[はつげん]が{物議[ぶつぎ]を醸[かも]して}いる。

ctx.en: With its graphic scenes, the film caused controversy even before its release.

ctx.s: 「あのコマーシャル、ネットで炎上[えんじょう]してるね」「うん、かなり{物議[ぶつぎ]を醸[かも]して}るみたい」

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]はあえて{物議[ぶつぎ]を醸[かも]す}ような作品[さくひん]を発表[はっぴょう]し続[つづ]けている。
ctx.en: He keeps deliberately putting out work that is bound to cause controversy.

bad.s: 新商品[しんしょうひん]が大人気[だいにんき]で、{物議[ぶつぎ]を醸[かも]した}。
bad.en: (meant: the new product was a huge hit and caused a sensation)

bad.s: 昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]をどこで食[た]べるか、友達[ともだち]と{物議[ぶつぎ]を醸[かも]して}喧嘩[けんか]になった。
bad.en: (meant: my friend and I argued over where to have lunch)
bad.why: It is public controversy set off by a statement or act, not a private argument between two people.

cards.mean: to compete fiercely
cards.lit: to grind away the shinogi, the raised ridge along a sword blade, as two swords clash again and again

use.how: AとBがしのぎを削る / 〜でしのぎを削る: rivals of similar strength competing hard for the same prize, market or title.

near.diff: 火花を散らす is a sharp, heated clash at one moment; しのぎを削る is a sustained, close contest between rivals.

cards.cue: Three convenience-store chains keep opening shops on the same street and launching rival lunch boxes every month, each trying to win the same customers.

cards.mean: to become conceited after success
cards.lit: to turn into a tengu, the long-nosed mountain spirit of folklore, with one's nose held high

use.how: Xは天狗になっている / 天狗になるな: said of someone who has grown full of themselves after praise or success.

cards.r: かんにんぶくろのおがきれる

cards.r: ひとすじなわではいかない

cards.mean: to be too heavy a responsibility

cards.t: 居ても立ってもいられない

cards.mean: to falsely accuse someone
cards.lit: to make someone wear wet clothes: to dress them in a guilt that is not theirs

use.how: Xに(Yの)濡れ衣を着せる; most often passive: 万引きの濡れ衣を着せられる. Always a false accusation; clearing it is 濡れ衣を晴らす.

cards.cue: A classmate broke the window, then told the teacher that you did it, and now you are the one in trouble.

ctx.s: 殺人[さつじん]の{濡[ぬ]れ衣[ぎぬ]を着[き]せられた}男[おとこ]が、二十年[にじゅうねん]後[ご]に無罪[むざい]となった。

bad.en: (meant: he really stole it, so the police charged him)

bad.en: (meant: I took the blame myself to protect my friend)
bad.why: Someone else puts a false accusation on you. Taking the blame yourself is tsumi o kaburu or migawari ni naru.

cards.mean: to be momentarily tempted into wrongdoing
cards.lit: a demon comes over you: an evil spirit slips into your mind for a moment

use.how: Usually past, as an explanation or excuse for one lapse: 魔が差した, つい魔が差して. Ranges from a midnight snack to a real offence.

near.diff: 出来心 is a noun for the sudden bad impulse itself (出来心で盗んだ); 魔が差す is the verb phrase for being seized by it.

cards.cue: A normally honest cashier explains why, that one time, she slipped a banknote from the till into her pocket.

ctx.en: Anyone can have a moment of weakness. Don't judge a person by one mistake.

ctx.en: I was about to put the wallet I'd found into my pocket when I caught myself. So this is what temptation feels like.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は三年間[さんねんかん]、計画的[けいかくてき]に会社[かいしゃ]のお金[かね]を盗[ぬす]み続[つづ]けた。{魔[ま]が差[さ]した}のだ。
bad.en: (meant: he systematically stole for three years; he was simply wicked)
bad.why: It is a single momentary impulse, not deliberate wrongdoing planned and repeated over years.

bad.s: 出[で]かけたら急[きゅう]に雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ってきて、{魔[ま]が差[さ]した}。
bad.en: (meant: I went out and bad luck struck when it suddenly rained)
bad.why: It is a wrong impulse inside your own mind, not misfortune that happens to you from outside.

cards.mean: to rack one's brains
cards.lit: to wring out your wisdom: squeeze your mind like a cloth for the last drop of ideas

use.how: Verb phrase, often with みんなで: thinking hard to find a way through a specific problem, especially under limits of money, time or space.

near.diff: 頭を抱える is being at a loss, stuck with a problem; 知恵を絞る is actively working hard to find a solution.

cards.cue: Your club has almost no budget, so everyone sits down together to come up with clever ways to hold the festival anyway.

ctx.s: 狭[せま]い部屋[へや]を広[ひろ]く使[つか]うために、{知恵[ちえ]を絞[しぼ]った}収納術[しゅうのうじゅつ]を紹介[しょうかい]します。

bad.en: (meant: I worked hard to memorise a hundred English words)

bad.s: 困[こま]っている後輩[こうはい]に{知恵[ちえ]を絞[しぼ]って}あげた。
bad.en: (meant: I gave my struggling junior some advice)
bad.why: Lending someone your ideas is chie o kasu. Chie o shiboru is your own hard thinking, not something you give to another person.

cards.mean: conversation becomes lively
cards.lit: flowers bloom on the conversation: the talk opens up and blossoms

use.how: Often with a topic before it: 思い出話に花が咲く, 昔話に花が咲く. Narrates a pleasant, lively chat among people, usually in the past tense.

near.diff: 話が弾む says a conversation flows easily; 話に花が咲く pictures a topic, often shared memories, blossoming into a long happy chat.
話が合う says two people have common ground to talk about; 話に花が咲く describes a particular chat turning lively.

cards.cue: At a class reunion, old friends start reminiscing about school days and keep talking happily for hours.

ctx.s: 久[ひさ]しぶりに会[あ]った友[とも]だちと、{話[はなし]に花[はな]が咲[さ]いた}。
ctx.en: With the friend I hadn't seen for ages, the conversation really took off.

ctx.s: 同窓会[どうそうかい]では、学生時代[がくせいじだい]の思[おも]い出[で]{話[ばなし]に花[はな]が咲[さ]いた}。

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]の家[いえ]に親戚[しんせき]が集[あつ]まると、いつも昔[むかし]{話[ばなし]に花[はな]が咲[さ]く}。

ctx.s: 旅行[りょこう]の計画[けいかく]を立[た]てるはずが、食[た]べ物[もの]の{話[はなし]に花[はな]が咲[さ]いて}、何[なに]も決[き]まらなかった。

bad.en: (meant: the principal gave a long speech on his own for an hour)
bad.why: It needs people chatting together. One person talking at an audience is not a conversation blooming.

cards.mean: to chime in to show one is listening
cards.lit: to strike the answering hammer blow

story.text: In a Japanese forge, the master smith and an assistant strike the hot metal in turn, the assistant's hammer answering the master's in a steady rhythm. That answering stroke was called aizuchi, the 'matching hammer'. The word came to mean the short replies a listener puts in to keep a speaker going.

use.how: Xに相槌を打つ: short listening signals (うん, へえ, なるほど) while someone talks. 適当に相槌を打つ means only pretending to listen.

near.diff: 口を挟む is cutting in with your own words or opinion; 相槌を打つ is supportive signals that keep the other person talking.

ctx.en: If you don't make listening noises on the phone, the other person gets uneasy.

ctx.en: "Are you actually listening?" "I am! Look, I'm going 'uh-huh', aren't I?"

bad.s: 会議[かいぎ]で反対[はんたい]意見[いけん]を言[い]うために、部長[ぶちょう]の話[はなし]に{相槌[あいづち]を打[う]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I cut in on the manager to voice my objection)
bad.why: Aizuchi are short supportive signals, not an interruption with your own opinion. Cutting in is kuchi o hasamu.

bad.s: 「どこに住[す]んでいますか」と聞[き]かれて、「大阪[おおさか]です」と{相槌[あいづち]を打[う]った}。
bad.en: (meant: when asked where I live, I answered 'Osaka')
bad.why: An aizuchi is a listening signal while someone else is talking, not an answer to a question.

cards.mean: things are taking an ominous turn
cards.lit: the movement of the clouds looks suspicious: the sky looks as if rain is coming

use.how: Predicate, often with なってきた: of the weather, or of a situation (talks, a match, the economy, a relationship) starting to look like trouble ahead.

ctx.en: The sky looks threatening, so let's take an umbrella.

ctx.en: My boyfriend has been replying less and less; things are starting to look shaky.

ctx.s: 「交渉[こうしょう]、うまくいってる？」「それが、ちょっと{雲行[くもゆ]きが怪[あや]しい}んだ。」
ctx.en: "Are the negotiations going well?" "Actually, things are starting to look a bit iffy."

ctx.s: 後半[こうはん]に二点[にてん]取[と]られ、試合[しあい]の{雲行[くもゆ]きが怪[あや]しくなってきた}。
ctx.en: After conceding two goals in the second half, the match started to turn against us.

ctx.s: 景気[けいき]の{雲行[くもゆ]きが怪[あや]しい}中[なか]、多[おお]くの企業[きぎょう]が採用[さいよう]を減[へ]らしている。
ctx.en: With dark clouds gathering over the economy, many companies are cutting back on hiring.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]が急[きゅう]に黙[だま]り込[こ]んだのを見[み]て、会議[かいぎ]の{雲行[くもゆ]きが怪[あや]しい}と感[かん]じた。
ctx.en: When the manager suddenly fell silent, I sensed the meeting was heading for trouble.

bad.en: (meant: his story sounds fishy, so I can't believe it)

bad.en: (meant: the company went bankrupt last month and things are bad now)
bad.why: It signals trouble that seems to be coming, like clouds before rain, not a disaster that has already happened.

cards.mean: starting before everything is ready
cards.lit: a departure after giving up on the rest: the train pulls out without waiting for everyone

story.text: The phrase began as railway language: when departure time came or a train was full, it pulled out even though not everyone waiting had got on, giving up on (mikiri) the rest. From there it came to mean pushing ahead with a decision or a project before discussion or preparation is complete.

use.how: Noun (見切り発車で始める, 見切り発車だ) or verb 見切り発車する. Mostly criticises a plan begun before preparation or agreement was complete.

near.diff: 見切りをつける is giving up on someone or something as hopeless; 見切り発車 is starting something before it is ready.

cards.cue: The company switched to the new system before testing was finished, and the staff still don't know how to use it.

ctx.en: Going ahead before we were properly prepared is why it failed.

ctx.en: The new system was launched before it was ready, and chaos followed on the ground.

ctx.en: "You're starting to build it before the specs are even settled? That's jumping the gun."

ctx.s: 全員[ぜんいん]の合意[ごうい]を待[ま]っていたら間[ま]に合[あ]わないので、{見切[みき]り発車[はっしゃ]する}ことにした。

ctx.en: The app, rushed out without enough testing, was full of bugs.

bad.en: (meant: the train left on schedule)
bad.why: It is not a normal departure: even in railway use it meant leaving waiting passengers behind, and today it is mostly figurative.

bad.en: (meant: I gave up on my dream of being a singer and took an office job)
bad.why: Giving up on something is mikiri o tsukeru. Mikiri hassha is starting something too early.
